g.text: 2. How rss_stat Maps Under the Hood

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The NR_MM_COUNTERS array slot indexes still track the same core residency metrics:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: MM_FILEPAGES: File-backed memory pages.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: MM_ANONPAGES: Anonymous memory pages (what you knew as anon_rss).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: MM_SWAPENTS: Pages that have been swapped out to disk.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: MM_SHMEMPAGES: Shared memory pages (IPC, shmget, anonymous MAP_SHARED).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: By changing this array to a per-CPU counter structure, a thread running on Core 0 increments Core 0's private count bucket. A thread on Core 128 increments Core 128's private bucket. No cross-talk, zero locks, and maximum execution speed on the hot allocation path.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 3. Reading the Value is No Longer Free

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Because the counter values are scattered across individual per-core structures, you can no longer read a simple member scalar from GDB or C code.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel's wrapper macro get_mm_counter(mm, member) now has to sum up the data across the core matrix:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: C

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: static inline unsigned long get_mm_counter(struct mm_struct *mm, int member)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: // Sums up the local counters across all CPUs, ensuring it doesn't return a negative fluke

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: return percpu_counter_sum_positive(&mm->rss_stat[member]);

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: (Note: In the newest hierarchical tree variants, this calls percpu_counter_tree_precise_sum_positive to aggregate data faster across NUMA nodes.)

g.text: data_vm

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel explicitly added this to track a process's private writable data space. Notice the logic gates: it

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: must be writable (VM_WRITE), but it cannot be a shared mapping (~VM_SHARED), and it cannot be the stack

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: (~VM_STACK).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel needs this field because of RLIMIT_DATA (the maximum size of a process's data segment). Every

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: time a process calls brk() or allocates anonymous private memory, the kernel verifies it against data_vm to

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: ensure the process isn't blowing past its system-enforced memory limits.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: pinned_vm

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: This tracks pages that have been locked into place using specialized kernel routines like pin_user_pages().

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Unlike locked_vm (which is triggered by userspace calling mlock() to prevent swapping), pinned_vm is used by

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: high-performance kernel subsystems—like RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) or Direct I/O.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a page is pinned, the kernel cannot move it at all (even for page migration or defragmentation), because

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: an external hardware device is actively reading or writing to that specific physical RAM address. Because multiple

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: threads can pin pages concurrently, this is tracked using an atomic type (atomic64_t) to prevent race conditions

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: without needing to lock the whole mm_struct.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fdt and fdtable

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fdt: This is the pointer the kernel actually uses whenever it looks up a file descriptor

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: (using macros like files_fdtable(files)). It points to a struct fdtable which contains the arrays of open files,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: close-on-exec flags, and bitmasks.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fdtab: This is an embedded, default fallback table.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Design Trick: When a process starts, fdt points directly to the internal fdtab right next to it.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: However, if your process opens a massive number of files that exceed the default limits, the kernel al

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: locates a brand new, larger struct fdtable on the heap, points fdt to that new heap address, and

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: leaves fdtab behind. This prevents a memory allocation penalty for normal processes while remaining infinitely scalable.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fd_array

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fd_array: This is a static array of pointers to struct file objects.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: On standard x86 architectures, NR_OPEN_DEFAULT is typically set to 32 or 64.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Because it's embedded right inside the structure, the pointers for standard descriptors—like 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), 2 (stderr),

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: and your initial opened files—are allocated in a single contiguous block of memory. The CPU can fetch these pointers incredibly fast without chasing heap pointers.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fdtable {

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: unsigned int max_fds (The absolute maximum capacity of the current arrays the kernel triggers a table resize if fds go beyond this.)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct file __rcu **fd (This is a pointer-to-pointers. It is an array where every slot contains a pointer to a struct file)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct rcu_head rcu

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: fd

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When the process starts, this fd pointer points right back into the small, embedded fd_array[]

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: inside the files_struct. If the process expands beyond that default size, fd is redirected to point

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: to a brand new, massive array allocated on the heap.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: rcu

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When the table resizes, the kernel allocates a new fdtable and instantly

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: changes the process's tracking pointer to look at the new one. However,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: other CPU cores might still be looking up a file in the old table at that

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: exact microsecond. The rcu_head is a tiny structure that tells the kernel:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: "Don't free this memory immediately. Wait until all active readers finish looking

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: up their files, then safely destroy this old table in the background."

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: f_inode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: In older kernels, the file structure pointed directly to the directory entry cache structure:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: To find the file metadata (the inode) from here, you had to dereference the dentry:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: file -> f_dentry -> d_inode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: To clean up how mount points and directories were tracked, the kernel engineers grouped the

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: dentry and the virtual filesystem mount point (vfsmount) into a unified helper structure

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: called struct path:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: During this cleanup, f_dentry was removed. To get the dentry, code had to change to:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: file -> f_path.dentry

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: And to get the inode, code had to jump twice:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: file -> f_path.dentry -> d_inode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Jumping from the file to the dentry, and then from the dentry to the inode is an

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: incredibly frequent operation. It happens on every single read, write, seek,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: and poll system call.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: On modern CPUs, chasing pointers across three different structures located

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: in different parts of system RAM often results in CPU L1/L2 cache misses.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: To optimize this hot-path, kernel developers did something simple: they added a

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: cached direct pointer right back into struct file:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct inode *f_inode;

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Now, if the kernel wants to read or write, it doesn't have to look up the dentry first.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: It immediately dereferences the cached f_inode pointer directly.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: vfsmount {

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct dentry *mnt_root (The dentry representing the directory that acts as the root of this specific mount)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct super_block *mnt_sb (A pointer to the physical file system's Superblock.)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: int mnt_flags (A bitmask controlling the specific security and operational behaviors enforced at the mount level. Common flags: MNT_READONLY, MNT_NOSUID, MNT_NODEV)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: i_no

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 1. The True Identity of a File

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: In Linux, file names do not matter to the operating system. File names are purely a user-friendly abstraction managed by the directory cache (struct dentry).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: To the kernel and the file system driver, the actual identity of a file is defined entirely by its inode number (i_ino).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If two different directory entries (dentry objects) point to two different filenames, but both reference the exact same i_ino on the same filesystem, you have a Hard Link.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The file's data block mapping, permissions, and size are shared instantly because they both share the exact same struct inode.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 2. Bridging the VFS to the Disk Blocks

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When your application requests data from a file descriptor, the VFS layer hands the operation off to the filesystem driver (like ext4 or btrfs). The driver reads i_ino to compute exactly where that file's metadata structure is located on the physical disk sectors.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: For example, in a traditional ext4 filesystem layout, the disk is divided into "Block Groups," each containing an Inode Table. The driver takes i_ino, calculates its offset within that table, and reads the raw metadata from the disk to populate the rest of the fields inside your struct inode object in RAM.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: inode {

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: u64 i_ino (This is the absolute, unique serial number assigned to a specific file or directory by the underlying filesystem)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: atomic_t i_count (Reference count — same `_refcount` discipline from `struct page`. Inode isn't freed while this is nonzero)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: unsigned int i_nlink (Number of hard links)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 1. kuid_t i_uid (Owner User ID)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: What it is: The unique identifier of the user who owns the file.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The k Prefix Significance: The kuid_t type stands for Kernel User ID.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel does not use raw integer UIDs directly here because of modern

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: features like user namespaces (containers). A user might be UID 0 (root)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: inside an unprivileged LXC/Docker container, but map to UID 100000 on the

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: physical host. kuid_t is a structure abstraction that handles this internal mapping safely.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 2. kgid_t i_gid (Owner Group ID)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: What it is: The identifier of the POSIX group assigned to the file.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The k Prefix Significance: Just like the UID, kgid_t stands for Kernel Group ID. It abstracts

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: the group integer across namespace boundaries to ensure that group permissions are safely

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: translated between host and containers.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 3. umode_t i_mode (File Type & Permissions Bitmask)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: What it is: A 16-bit bitmask that stores two critical pieces of data packed together: the file

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: type and the access permissions (what you see when running ls -l).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Internal Bit Layout:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Top 4 bits (File Type): Identifies what kind of inode this is (e.g., standard file, directory,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: symbolic link, socket, block device). The kernel checks these bits using macros like S_ISREG() or S_ISDIR().

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Bottom 12 bits (Flags & Permissions):

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 3 bits for execution flags: SUID (Set User ID), SGID (Set Group ID), and the Sticky Bit.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 9 bits for standard POSIX permissions: User (rwx), Group (rwx), and Others (rwx).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: How the Kernel Evaluates Them Together

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a process tries to open a file, the VFS layer calls a helper function (typically generic_permission()) that uses

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: these three exact fields in a strict cascading order:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: [ Process attempts to access file ]

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: ├──► Is Process UID == inode->i_uid?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: │ YES ──► Check User bits in i_mode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: ├──► Is Process GID matching inode->i_gid?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: │ YES ──► Check Group bits in i_mode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: └──► Otherwise ─────────────────────────► Check Other bits in i_mode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Hard Links and Symlinks

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 1. Hard Links: Multiple Names, Same Inode

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A hard link is just an additional directory entry (struct dentry) pointing to an existing inode number

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: (i_ino) on the same filesystem.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Under the Hood: When you create a hard link, the kernel allocates a new dentry with the new filename,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: but it copies the exact same i_ino into it. It also increments the reference counter (i_nlink) inside the struct inode.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Behavior: Both filenames are completely identical peers. If you delete the original filename, the inode and

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: the file data remain completely intact because i_nlink is still greater than 0. The data is only wiped from the disk when all hard links are deleted.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Limitations: Because an inode number is only unique within its own filesystem partition, hard links cannot cross filesystem

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: boundaries (e.g., you cannot hard link a file from an ext4 drive onto a btrfs drive). You also cannot hard link directories (to prevent infinite loops in the filesystem graph).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: [dentry: file.txt] ─────► i_ino = 142857 ────► [ struct inode ] ──► Data Blocks

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: [dentry: hardlink.txt] ────────┘ (Points directly to the same Inode)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 2. Symbolic Links (Symlinks): A Shortcut File

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: A symlink is a completely distinct, special type of file that contains a text string pointing to the path of another filename.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Under the Hood: When you create a symlink, the kernel allocates a brand new inode with its own unique i_ino and a

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: distinct struct inode. The file type bits in i_mode are set to S_IFLNK (Symbolic Link). The data blocks of this new i

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: node simply store the text path string of the target file (e.g., "/home/user/file.txt").

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Behavior: When a process tries to open a symlink, the VFS layer reads the path string stored inside the symlink's inode,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: halts the current lookup, and restarts the path resolution algorithm using the target path. If you delete the original

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: target file, the symlink remains but becomes "broken" (pointing to a path that no longer exists).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Advantages: Because it relies entirely on a text path string, symlinks can span across different physical drives and file

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: systems, and they can point directly to directories without restrictions.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: [dentry: symlink.txt] ──► i_ino = 999999 ──► [struct inode (S_IFLNK)] ──► Data: "file.txt"

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: [dentry: file.txt] ─────► i_ino = 142857 ──────────────────────────────► [struct inode] ──► Data Blocks

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Wy

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Why inode stores i_fop as well? (To be explored further)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The short answer: The inode's f_op acts as the master template that dictates how a file descriptor should behave

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: when it is first opened.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Here is the exact architectural reason for this design:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 1. The Polymorphism Problem: Not All Inodes are Disk Files

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: In Linux, an inode doesn't just represent a plain text file on an ext4 drive. An inode can represent a directory, a pipe (FIFO),

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: a network socket, or a character device (like a mouse or a GPU driver in /dev).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Each of these file types requires radically different operations when you call system calls like read() or write():

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Reading a regular file copies bytes from a storage driver's page cache.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Reading a network socket pulls packets from a network interface buffer.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Reading a character device executes custom code inside a hardware driver.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel needs a way to store which behavior belongs to this entry before anyone even opens it. That is the job of the

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: inode's operations pointer.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 2. The Initialization Hook (Setting up struct file)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a process calls open(), the kernel sets up a brand new struct file instance. But how does that new struct file know which

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: read and write functions to use?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: It copies them directly from the inode. The path looks like this:

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: // Simplified kernel logic inside the open system call path

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: file->f_op = inode->i_fop;

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: if (file->f_op->open) {

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: error = file->f_op->open(inode, file); // Trigger custom open routine

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: 3. The Power of Overriding (The Character Device Example)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The most elegant aspect of this architecture is how the kernel handles hardware drivers via Device Files (like /dev/nvme0).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When the filesystem mounts /dev, it creates inodes on the disk space. Initially, the generic filesystem driver assigns a

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: default device-file operation pointer to inode->i_fop.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a process opens /dev/nvme0, the generic open function triggers. It looks at the inode's device major/minor numbers,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: realizes it's a character device, and swaps the generic operations pointer out for the actual custom driver operations written

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: by the hardware manufacturer.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Any subsequent read() or write() calls on that file descriptor instantly route directly into the custom hardware driver code,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: completely bypassing the standard filesystem code.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: address_space {

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct inode *host (Back-pointer to the owning inode. NULL if not inode-backed (e.g. swapper's anonymous pages)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct xarray i_pages (Enhancement of old radix tree page_tree, representation of pages owned by this file)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: unsigned long nrpages (Total pages currently cached for this file)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: struct rb_root_cached i_mmap (Represents all userspace processes (VMA's) that have this page cache mapped into their address space)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: const struct address_space_operations *a_ops (Operations table for address_space)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: pgoff_t writeback_index (Where writeback left off — used to resume flushing dirty pages sequentially )

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: i_mmap and i_pages

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: To see how i_pages (the XArray) and i_mmap (the cached Red-Black tree) differ, you have to look at the two completely different directions memory flows when a file is memory-mapped (mmap).

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Both live inside struct address_space, but they solve opposite problems. One handles the data, and the other handles the sharing processes.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Short Answer

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: i_pages (XArray): Maps a file offset to the physical memory pages (Folios) containing the data. It asks: "Where is the actual data for page index 5 in RAM?"

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: i_mmap (RB-Tree): Maps the file to all the userspace processes (vm_area_structs) that currently have this file mapped into their virtual memory. It asks: "Which processes are currently looking at this file?"

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Why i_mmap Needs a Red-Black Tree

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When you memory-map a file, you aren't loading the whole file into a process's memory at once. Instead, the kernel creates a vm_area_struct (VMA) in your process that points to a specific range of the file.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: If ten different processes map different parts of the same massive database file, the kernel needs a fast way to track all those different processes and their overlapping view windows. That is what i_mmap does.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: It uses an augmented Red-Black tree (rb_root_cached) to store intervals of VMAs sorted by their file offsets.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The Dynamic Interaction (When they meet)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The easiest way to understand the difference is to trace what happens during a Page Fault or a Cache Eviction. This is where the two structures talk to each other.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Scenario A: Reading/Writing Data (Using i_pages)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: When a process reads from a memory-mapped file address and the data isn't in RAM yet, a page fault triggers. The kernel looks inside i_pages (XArray) using the file offset. If it's a miss, it reads the data from disk,

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: allocates a physical page, and drops it into i_pages.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: Scenario B: Unmapping or Evicting (Using i_mmap)

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: What happens if the system runs out of memory, and the kernel needs to evict a dirty file page from RAM? Or what if a process calls msync() to flush changes back to disk?

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel has the physical page, but it needs to find every single process table entry pointing to it to clear the "Present" bit.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: The kernel looks at the page and finds its address_space.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: It looks at i_mmap (RB-Tree) to search for all process VMAs that cover this specific file offset.

text.font-family: Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji
Excalifont, Xiaolai, sans-serif, Segoe UI Emoji

g.text: It walks down those specific VMAs, unmaps the page from those processes' page tables, and then safely frees the physical page from i_pages.
